title: Marx: Alienation, Class and History
subtitle: Philosophers have interpreted the world; the point is to change it
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain historical materialism and the metaphor of base and superstructure.
By the end you will be able to describe the four forms of alienated labor in Marx's 1844 Manuscripts.
By the end you will be able to summarize Marx's account of class struggle and his critique of capitalism, including surplus value.
By the end you will be able to explain how Marx transformed Hegel's dialectic.
By the end you will be able to weigh Marx's lasting insights against his failed predictions and the record of regimes that claimed his name.
hook:
In Highgate Cemetery in north London stands a large stone monument topped with a bronze bust of a bearded man. Carved on it are two sentences. The first: “Workers of all lands unite.” The second: “The philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways. The point however is to change it.” When Karl Marx was buried there in March 1883, only about a dozen people attended the funeral. Within a century, governments ruling roughly a third of humanity claimed to be guided by his ideas.

Few thinkers have changed the world as directly, or been blamed for as much. To some, Marx is the prophet of liberation from exploitation; to others, the intellectual godfather of the gulag. Both reactions can make it hard to see what he actually argued. Today we set the legend aside and look at the philosopher: a former student of Hegel (Day 59) who asked why, in the richest society in history, so many people felt their work, their lives and even their own humanity were not their own. His questions about labor, class and power remain urgent even for those who reject his answers.

sections.heading: From Young Hegelian to Revolutionary Exile
sections.body:
Karl Marx was born in 1818 in Trier, in the Prussian Rhineland, into a family descended from rabbis on both sides; his father converted to Lutheranism, probably to keep his career as a lawyer under Prussian restrictions on Jews. Marx studied law in Bonn and Berlin, but in Berlin he fell under the spell of Hegel's philosophy and joined the **Young Hegelians**, radical students who used Hegel's ideas to criticize religion and the Prussian state (recall the Left Hegelians from Day 59). His doctoral dissertation, completed in 1841, compared the atomic theories of Democritus and Epicurus, whom you met on Days 7 and 24.

Blocked from an academic career because of his radical views, Marx became a journalist, editing a liberal newspaper in Cologne until the authorities shut it down in 1843. He moved to Paris, where in 1844 he met Friedrich Engels, the son of a German textile manufacturer who managed a family mill in Manchester. Engels had just written a searing account of *The Condition of the Working Class in England*. The two became lifelong collaborators. Engels would support Marx financially for decades.

Expelled from Paris, Marx moved to Brussels, where in early 1848 he and Engels published the *Manifesto of the Communist Party*. Revolutions swept across Europe that year, then failed. In 1849 Marx went into exile in London, where he would spend the rest of his life. The family lived for years in poverty in Soho; several of his children died young. Marx spent long days in the Reading Room of the British Museum, studying economics. The first volume of his masterpiece, *Capital*, appeared in 1867. He died in 1883, leaving the second and third volumes to be edited and published by Engels.

One point about sources matters. Many of Marx's most philosophical writings, including the *Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844* and *The German Ideology*, were not published until the twentieth century, in the 1930s. So the Marx known to early Marxists was mostly the economist of *Capital* and the revolutionary of the *Manifesto*. The humanist Marx of alienation was rediscovered later, and that rediscovery reshaped how his work was read.

sections.heading: Standing Hegel on His Feet: Historical Materialism
sections.body:
Marx took from Hegel the idea that history develops through conflict and contradiction toward freedom. But he thought Hegel had the story upside down. For Hegel, the driving force was Spirit, ideas coming to know themselves. In a famous image from the afterword to the second edition of *Capital*, Marx wrote that in Hegel the dialectic is standing on its head; it must be turned right side up again to discover the rational kernel within the mystical shell.

What stands on the ground, for Marx, is **material life**: how human beings produce what they need to survive. Before people can do philosophy, religion or politics, they must eat, find shelter and make clothes. How a society organizes this production shapes everything else. This view is called **historical materialism** (a term Engels popularized). Here *materialism* does not mean a love of possessions, and it is not quite the atomism of Democritus either. It means that the economic organization of society is the foundation of social life and historical change.

In the preface to *A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy* (1859), Marx summarized the theory with a building metaphor. The **base** of society consists of its **forces of production** (tools, technology, skills, raw materials) and its **relations of production** (who owns what, who works for whom). On top of this base rises a **superstructure** of law, politics, religion, art and philosophy. He put the point in a much-quoted sentence: it is not the consciousness of men that determines their being, but their social being that determines their consciousness.

History moves, Marx argued, when the forces of production outgrow the relations of production. Feudal relations of lords and serfs eventually became fetters on the growing power of trade and manufacture, and they were burst apart by the rise of the merchant and industrial class, the **bourgeoisie**. In the same way, he predicted, capitalist relations would one day become fetters on the immense productive power capitalism itself had created.

Scholars still argue about how strict this determinism is. Is the superstructure merely a reflection of the base? Late in life, Engels insisted that the economy is determining only in the last instance, and that law, ideas and politics react back on it. The relationship is better seen as one of strong influence than of simple mechanical cause.

sections.heading: Alienated Labor
sections.body:
In the *1844 Manuscripts*, the young Marx asked a question that sounds surprisingly personal. Why does work under capitalism so often feel like a curse? His answer is the theory of **alienation** (*Entfremdung*, literally becoming-a-stranger).

The starting point is a view of human nature. Marx thought humans are distinctive in producing freely and consciously. A bee builds a hive by instinct; a human architect first builds the structure in imagination, then realizes it in the world. Through creative labor we express ourselves and transform nature into a mirror of our own powers. Remember Hegel's slave, who found himself in the things he made (Day 59). Marx calls this capacity our **species-being** (*Gattungswesen*).

Under capitalism, he argued, this creative activity is turned against the worker in four ways:

1. **Alienation from the product.** What the worker makes belongs to someone else, the owner, and confronts the worker as an alien power. The more she produces, the more wealth she creates for others.

2. **Alienation from the activity of labor.** Work is not chosen or self-directed; it is forced labor, a mere means to survive. The worker, Marx observed, feels himself only outside his work, and in his work feels outside himself. He feels most free in his animal functions (eating, drinking, sleeping) and most like an animal in his human function, work.

3. **Alienation from species-being.** Because labor is reduced to a means of survival, the very capacity that makes us human becomes a mere tool for keeping alive.

4. **Alienation from other people.** Relations between people become relations of competition and exchange; the worker faces the capitalist, and other workers, as rivals or instruments.

Think of a worker on a factory assembly line in Marx's time, repeating one motion for twelve hours, never seeing the finished product, owning none of it, and replaceable at any moment. Marx's point is not only that this is painful but that it is *dehumanizing*: it cuts people off from what makes them human. In later writings, especially *Capital*, he developed a related idea, **commodity fetishism**: in a market society, relations between people (who made what, under what conditions) appear as relations between things and their prices, hiding the human labor behind them.

sections.heading: Class Struggle and the Critique of Capitalism
sections.body:
The *Communist Manifesto* opens its first section with a sweeping claim: “The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.” Free men and slaves, lords and serfs, guild masters and journeymen: in each era an exploiting class and an exploited class have stood in constant opposition. Modern society, the *Manifesto* says, has simplified this conflict into two great camps: the **bourgeoisie**, who own the **means of production** (factories, machines, land), and the **proletariat**, who own nothing but their ability to work and must sell it for wages.

One surprising feature of the *Manifesto* is its admiration for capitalism. The bourgeoisie, Marx and Engels wrote, had created more massive and more colossal productive forces than all preceding generations together. It had swept away feudal ties, created a world market, and transformed every country. Its restlessness was unprecedented: all that is solid melts into air. Marx was not nostalgic for village life. He thought capitalism was a necessary stage that made a free society possible.

Why, then, is capitalism exploitative? In *Capital*, Marx developed the theory of **surplus value**, building on the labor theory of value of earlier economists like Adam Smith and David Ricardo. A worker sells the capitalist her **labor power**, her capacity to work for a day, and is paid roughly what it costs to keep her alive and working. But during that day she produces goods worth more than her wage. Suppose she produces the equivalent of her wages in six hours but works ten. The extra four hours create surplus value, which the capitalist keeps as profit. No one is cheating in the ordinary sense; the wage is a fair market price. Yet the system as a whole rests, Marx argued, on the unpaid labor of the many.

Marx predicted that competition would drive capitalists to cut wages and replace workers with machines, concentrating wealth in fewer hands, producing recurrent crises, and swelling the ranks of an increasingly impoverished proletariat. Eventually the workers, made conscious of their shared situation, would overthrow the system. What would follow? Marx said surprisingly little. He wrote of a transitional dictatorship of the proletariat and, eventually, a classless society in which the state would wither away, governed by the principle, from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs (*Critique of the Gotha Programme*, 1875). Religion, which he famously called the opium of the people, the sigh of the oppressed creature, would fade once people no longer needed its consolations.

sections.heading: Legacy and Failures
sections.body:
Any honest assessment of Marx must face two facts at once: the power of many of his insights and the failure of many of his predictions, together with the catastrophic record of regimes that ruled in his name.

**Failed predictions.** Marx expected revolution first in the most advanced industrial countries, such as Britain and Germany. Instead, communist revolutions came in largely agrarian societies: Russia in 1917, China in 1949. In the industrial West, workers' living standards rose substantially, partly through trade unions, the vote and welfare states, rather than sinking into ever deeper misery. The middle classes grew rather than vanishing. Karl Popper (Day 72) also argued that Marxists repeatedly reinterpreted their theory to avoid refutation, making it unfalsifiable and therefore unscientific.

**The communist record.** Under Lenin, Stalin, Mao and others, one-party states abolished political freedom, persecuted dissidents, and built systems of forced labor camps. Man-made famines, including the Soviet famine of 1932–33 (which devastated Ukraine, where it is known as the Holodomor) and the famine of China's Great Leap Forward (1959–61), killed millions; historians' estimates for the Chinese famine alone commonly run to tens of millions. Is Marx responsible? Scholars disagree. Defenders note that he never designed a one-party police state and wrote of human emancipation. Critics reply that his contempt for liberal rights as merely bourgeois, his confidence in the inevitable direction of history, and his talk of a dictatorship of the proletariat left the door open. At the very least, his vagueness about how a post-capitalist society would actually work left a vacuum that authoritarians filled.

**Lasting insights.** Even many non-Marxists credit Marx with ideas that became permanent parts of modern thought: that economic interests shape law, politics and culture; that technology transforms society; that markets can concentrate wealth and power; that crises are recurrent features of capitalism; that work can be meaningful or dehumanizing depending on how it is organized. Modern sociology, economic history and labor studies all carry his mark. The Frankfurt School (Day 80) developed his ideas into critical theory, and his account of alienation influenced existentialists like Sartre (Day 77).

The right lesson may be that Marx was a brilliant diagnostician and a poor prophet. His description of the restless, world-transforming power of capitalism reads as remarkably modern. His cure, in practice, proved far worse than the disease.

keyQuote.text: The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point is to change it.
keyQuote.source: Karl Marx, Theses on Feuerbach (1845), Thesis XI

modernConnection.title: Alienation in the Gig Economy
modernConnection.body:
Picture a delivery rider in a modern city. An app assigns her jobs, sets her pay per delivery, tracks her route in real time, rates her speed, and can deactivate her account without a human conversation. She is officially an independent contractor, not an employee, so she may lack sick pay or a pension. She never meets her boss, because her boss is, in practice, an algorithm.

Marx's categories fit uncomfortably well. Alienation from the activity of labor: the pace and form of work are dictated by software designed by others. Alienation from other workers: riders compete for jobs and ratings, scattered across a city with few chances to organize. Commodity fetishism: when you tap a button and food appears, the human labor, the rain, the traffic and the low pay are invisible behind a price and a smooth interface. Researchers studying warehouse work, content moderation and click work describe similar patterns of **algorithmic management**, in which every second is measured and optimized.

The broader conversation echoes Marx too. Surveys about burnout, disengagement and “quiet quitting” suggest that many people experience their jobs as something done only for the paycheck, the feeling Marx described as being at home only outside work. Debates about the share of income going to wages versus profits, and about how much wealth is concentrated among the richest, keep his questions about distribution alive. Even technology firms that market themselves as giving users free services fit a Marxian pattern in a new way: some critics argue that users' attention and data are the real product being sold.

But the comparison has limits. Many gig workers value the flexibility, and most people in market economies live far longer, healthier and wealthier lives than Marx's factory workers did, a fact his prediction of ever-deepening misery did not anticipate. Many people do find meaning in their jobs, and reforms within capitalism, such as labor laws, unions and court rulings about gig workers' employment status, have addressed some abuses without revolution. Marx helps us see what is troubling in modern work; he does not settle what we should do about it.

vocabulary.definition: Marx's theory that the way a society organizes material production is the foundation of its social life and the main driver of historical change.
vocabulary.example: A historical materialist would explain the end of feudalism by changes in trade and production, not mainly by new ideas.

vocabulary.definition: Marx's metaphor in which the economic base (forces and relations of production) shapes the superstructure of law, politics, religion and culture.
vocabulary.example: On the base and superstructure model, property laws tend to reflect the interests of the class that owns the means of production.

vocabulary.definition: For Marx, the condition in which workers are estranged from the products of their labor, their own activity, their human nature and one another.
vocabulary.example: A worker who spends every day on one repetitive task, owning nothing she makes, illustrates Marx's idea of alienation.

vocabulary.definition: Marx's term for the distinctively human capacity for free, conscious, creative production through which we express our nature.
vocabulary.example: For Marx, a craftsman designing and building a table expresses his species-being.

vocabulary.definition: The class that owns the means of production (bourgeoisie) and the class that owns only its labor power and must work for wages (proletariat).
vocabulary.example: In Marx's analysis, a factory owner belongs to the bourgeoisie and the factory's wage workers to the proletariat.

vocabulary.definition: The value workers produce beyond what they are paid in wages, which the capitalist keeps as profit; for Marx, the source of exploitation.
vocabulary.example: If a worker produces her wage's worth in six hours but works ten, Marx would say the remaining four hours create surplus value.

vocabulary.definition: Marx's term for the way market societies make relations between people appear as relations between things and their prices, hiding the labor behind products.
vocabulary.example: Buying a cheap shirt without thinking about who sewed it, and under what conditions, illustrates commodity fetishism.

vocabulary.definition: The tools, machines, factories, land and raw materials used to produce goods.
vocabulary.example: For Marx, who owns the means of production determines who holds power in a society.

thinkingExercise.title: An Alienation Audit
thinkingExercise.prompt: Marx claims that work can either express our humanity or estrange us from it. Spend 10–15 minutes examining a job you have held (paid or unpaid, including study or household work) through his four forms of alienation, and then test his theory.
steps: Describe the work briefly: what did you do, for whom, and who owned what you produced?

Rate it from 1 (not at all) to 5 (completely) on each of Marx's four forms: alienation from the product, from the activity, from your creative human capacities, and from other people. Give one concrete example for each rating.

Identify which features of the work caused the highest scores. Were they caused by ownership and class, as Marx argues, or by something else (technology, bureaucracy, the nature of the task, your own choices)?
Imagine one realistic change that would reduce alienation in that job. Would it require changing who owns the means of production, or could it happen within a market economy?
Finally, write a short judgment: is Marx's diagnosis of work still accurate, partly accurate, or outdated? What does your answer suggest about his proposed cure?

summary: Marx (1818–1883), a former Young Hegelian, kept Hegel's dialectic of history but grounded it in material production rather than Spirit.
Historical materialism holds that the economic base shapes the superstructure of law, politics and ideas, and that history moves through class struggle.
In the 1844 Manuscripts, Marx described four forms of alienated labor: from the product, the activity, our species-being and other people.
Capital analyzes exploitation through surplus value: workers produce more value than they are paid, and the difference becomes profit.
Marx admired capitalism's productive power but predicted its collapse into a classless society, a prediction that largely failed.
Regimes claiming his name caused immense suffering; scholars debate his responsibility, while many of his diagnostic insights remain influential.

quiz.question: How did Marx transform Hegel's dialectic?
options: He abandoned the idea that history develops at all
He replaced Spirit with material production as the driving force of history
He made religion the foundation of social change
He argued that history moves in an endless circle
quiz.explanation: Marx said Hegel's dialectic stood on its head; he grounded historical change in how humans produce their material lives.

quiz.question: In Marx's base and superstructure model, which of the following belongs to the superstructure?
options: Factories and machines
The relationship between employers and wage workers
Raw materials such as coal and iron
Law, religion and political ideas
quiz.explanation: The base consists of the forces and relations of production; law, politics, religion and philosophy form the superstructure.

quiz.question: A call center employee follows a strict script, is timed on every call, owns nothing she produces, and competes with colleagues for bonuses. Which Marxian concept best describes her situation?
options: Alienated labor
The owl of Minerva
The hedonic calculus
The categorical imperative
quiz.explanation: She is estranged from her activity, her product and her coworkers, which are among Marx's forms of alienation.

quiz.question: What is surplus value, according to Marx?
options: The extra price a shop charges during a shortage
Money saved by workers in a bank
The value workers produce beyond their wages, which the capitalist keeps as profit
The value of goods left unsold at the end of the year
quiz.explanation: Workers are paid for their labor power, but produce more value than their wages; the difference is surplus value, the source of profit.

quiz.question: Which statement about the Communist Manifesto is accurate?
options: It condemns capitalism as unproductive and backward
It praises capitalism's enormous productive power while predicting its overthrow
It recommends a return to feudal village life
It argues that class conflict ended with the French Revolution
quiz.explanation: Marx and Engels marveled that the bourgeoisie had created more productive forces than all preceding generations, yet predicted its downfall.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a prediction of Marx's that largely failed?
options: That capitalism would create a world market
That technology would transform society
That capitalist economies would experience recurring crises
That revolution would come first in the most advanced industrial countries and workers would grow ever poorer
quiz.explanation: Communist revolutions occurred in largely agrarian Russia and China, while workers' living standards in industrial countries rose.

quiz.question: What does Marx mean by commodity fetishism?
options: An obsessive desire to collect luxury goods
The way market prices make relations between people appear as relations between things, hiding the labor behind products
The religious worship of objects in pre-industrial societies
The government's control over the price of goods
quiz.explanation: In a market, products seem to have value in themselves; the social relations of labor that produced them disappear from view.

quiz.question: Marx's doctoral dissertation compared the natural philosophies of Democritus and Epicurus.
quiz.explanation: His 1841 dissertation examined the difference between the atomism of Democritus and that of Epicurus.

quiz.question: The Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, with their theory of alienation, were widely read by Marx's followers during his lifetime.
quiz.explanation: They were not published until the 1930s, so the humanist Marx of alienation was largely rediscovered in the twentieth century.

quiz.question: Marx provided a detailed blueprint for how a communist society and its government should be organized.
quiz.explanation: Marx said surprisingly little about post-capitalist society beyond broad phrases, a vagueness critics say left room for authoritarian regimes.

goDeeper.body:
Is there one Marx or two? In the mid-twentieth century, after the *1844 Manuscripts* were published, many thinkers, including existentialists and the Frankfurt School, embraced a **humanist Marx** whose central concern was alienation and human freedom. The French philosopher Louis Althusser objected that there was an **epistemological break** around 1845: the mature Marx of *Capital* abandoned the vague humanist idea of human essence for a scientific analysis of social structures. Most scholars today see more continuity than Althusser allowed; the idea of alienation reappears in *Capital* as commodity fetishism.

In the English-speaking world, a movement called **analytical Marxism** tried to restate Marx's ideas with the rigor of analytic philosophy and economics. G. A. Cohen's *Karl Marx's Theory of History: A Defence* (1978) offered a precise version of historical materialism using functional explanation: relations of production exist because they promote the development of productive forces. Others, like Jon Elster, criticized this and kept only what survived careful scrutiny. Cohen's later work turned to the ethics of equality, asking, in *Why Not Socialism?* (2009), whether the egalitarian spirit of a camping trip among friends could ever scale up to a society.

The economics also remains contested. Most economists reject the labor theory of value in favor of theories based on supply, demand and marginal utility, which weakens the technical argument for surplus value. Yet the question of whether capitalist inequality tends to grow over time was revived by Thomas Piketty's *Capital in the Twenty-First Century* (2013), which, though not Marxist in method, gave new data to an old worry. Ask yourself which parts of Marx depend on his economics, and which, like alienation, could stand on their own.

readings.title: The Marx-Engels Reader
readings.author: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (ed. Robert C. Tucker)
readings.note: A standard anthology including the 1844 Manuscripts, Theses on Feuerbach, the Manifesto and selections from Capital.

readings.title: Why Read Marx Today?
readings.author: Jonathan Wolff
readings.note: A short, balanced introduction by a non-Marxist philosopher on what remains valuable and what does not.

readings.title: Karl Marx: Greatness and Illusion
readings.author: Gareth Stedman Jones
readings.note: A major biography that places Marx firmly in his nineteenth-century context and separates him from later Marxism.

readings.title: Main Currents of Marxism
readings.author: Leszek Kołakowski
readings.note: A monumental critical history by a former Marxist; the third volume examines the path to Soviet and Chinese communism.

questions: Can Marx's theory of alienation be accepted even by someone who rejects his economics and his politics?
How much responsibility does a thinker bear for what others later do in their name?
Is work necessary for a meaningful human life, as Marx believed, or could a future with far less work also be fully human?
